paras: The attempted lynching of J. T. Wolck took place on April 9, 1888, when about forty workmen at the H. F. Shufeldt & Co. distillery in Chicago seized a private detective, also named as John T. Walck, and put a rope around his neck, saying he was spying for the whisky trust. Thomas Lynch, a partner in the firm, stopped the hanging, and the detective was tied to a post, made to swear a statement before a notary public, and driven into the street. Papers across the country carried it as a sidelight on the trust's campaign against an independent distillery.

Shufeldt's distillery, on Larrabee street near Chicago avenue, was described as the only one north of the Ohio River outside the whisky trust, which its proprietors said had tried "every means, both fair and foul" to ruin it. The proprietors said a Stanley detective had copied a customer's address from a shipment, after which a trust distillery in Peoria offered that customer gin below Shufeldt's price. The firm consulted lawyers and was told it had no adequate legal redress against the detective or his employers.

On the morning of April 9 the detective asked Thomas Lynch, the junior partner, for work and was hired, though the other employees had been told who he was. Soon afterward he was seen noting consignees' addresses in a notebook, and a workman seized him as a trust spy. The workmen knocked him down and took away a revolver he tried to draw, and the Narragansett Herald's version adds that he received "numerous kicks."

Men shouted "Hang the spy," and in the Macon Beacon's version the cries were "Kill him, string him up; don't let him out here alive." According to the Indianapolis Journal and the Illinois Staats-Zeitung, a rope was tied around his neck and the other end thrown over a beam, while the shorter wire said the rope was still being put on when a proprietor stepped in. Lynch stopped the hanging, and the detective, begging for his life, was tied to a post instead.

Before a notary public he swore to a statement, which in the Journal's account claimed he was checking for internal-revenue evasion and in the Herald's named his employers. He was then sent into the street with kicks after Lynch warned him that he would be shot if caught within a mile of the building. Only the Herald's version reported that the workmen threw stones after him as he fled.

No report of an arrest, a charge or a lawsuit against the workmen or the detective appears in the coverage. The distillery employees said they would "certainly hang the next spy they catch," and the Macon Beacon attributed a similar warning to Lynch.

The story first appeared on April 10 in Chicago's German daily, the Illinois Staats-Zeitung, and in papers elsewhere carrying a short wire or a longer Chicago special. The Waterbury Evening Democrat headed the wire "A Lynching Bee Prevented," and the Press and Daily Dakotaian ran the same text as "A Poor Place for Spies." The longer special, printed by the Indianapolis Journal, the New York Sun and the Richmond Dispatch, gave the proprietors' side at length and called the trust's tactics "the old Standard Oil method of stopping competition."

Some headlines put the blame on the trust: the Indiana State Sentinel ran "The Whisky Pool's Dirty Methods," and the Staats-Zeitung headed its local report "Wie es einem Spion erging" ("How a spy fared"). The New York Evening World and the Washington Evening Star gave it one sentence, and the St. Paul Daily Globe joked that "it is dangerous to touch Chicago people in a tender spot." A boilerplate version headed "A Spy Nearly Hanged" circulated in weeklies through late April, from Rhode Island to North and South Carolina.

The detective's name appeared as John T. Walck in the short wire and the Macon Beacon, J. T. Wolck in the Staats-Zeitung and the Herald, and J. F. Wolck or Wolcke in the Sentinel and the Dispatch. Printings of the Chicago special also differed in detail, the Journal dating the copied address March 30 where the Dispatch and the Staats-Zeitung gave March 20.

bases: About forty distillery workmen seized a detective, shouted to hang him and put a rope around his neck before a partner stopped them; it was an attempted lynching with no death (A3, A5, A12).
Forty workmen acting without lawful authority tried to hang the detective as a punishment for spying, but a partner stopped them and he left alive, so no one was killed (A3, A8, A12).
A Chicago German local report, a Chicago special, a short wire and a separate Chicago dispatch agree on the seizure, the rope and the rescue by a partner (A5, A3, A2, A11).

accounts.label: Proprietors' account (Chicago special)
accounts.gist: The firm said the trust had used Stanley's detectives to find and undersell its customers; the detective was caught noting consignees, had a rope tied round his neck over a beam, was saved by Lynch and swore he was checking internal-revenue compliance.

accounts.label: Chicago German local report
accounts.gist: The Staats-Zeitung told the same story with a noose over a beam, Lynch calming the men, a sworn written confession of Stanley's plan and a seized notebook, and said the workers felt their jobs threatened.

accounts.label: Short wire
accounts.gist: Workmen forced Walck under a beam and were putting a rope round his neck when a proprietor rescued him; after a written statement he was allowed to leave.

accounts.label: 'Spy Captured' dispatch
accounts.gist: Men cried 'Kill him, string him up' and were preparing to place a rope around his neck when Lynch saved him; he said he was looking for revenue-law violations and knew nothing of the trust.

accounts.label: 'A Spy Nearly Hanged' boilerplate
accounts.gist: Forty workmen knocked him down, kicked him and threw a rope around his neck until the proprietors interfered; he named his employers before a notary and was kicked out and stoned.

framing.detail: The wire ran as 'A Lynching Bee Prevented' and 'A Poor Place for Spies', ending with the workmen's vow to hang the next spy.
The Chicago special, headed 'A Detective in Danger', took the proprietors' view of the trust ('the old Standard Oil method') while describing the attempted hanging in dramatic dialogue.
The Indiana State Sentinel's headline 'The Whisky Pool's Dirty Methods' aimed its blame at the trust, not the workmen.
The Staats-Zeitung mocked the spy as a 'Schlaumeier' and headed its report 'Der Schnaps-Trust gründlch blamirt'.
The St. Paul Daily Globe treated the escape as a joke about Chicago touchiness.

conflicts.note: The Chicago German local report and the boilerplate agree on J. T. Wolck; the short wire has John T. Walck.
